short: A torpedoed liner, 1,198 dead, and the slow turn of American opinion towards war.
full:
On 7 May 1915 the Cunard liner Lusitania was eleven miles off the Old Head of Kinsale, inbound from New York, when the submarine U-20 fired a single torpedo into her starboard side. A second, larger internal explosion followed, and she listed so heavily that most of her lifeboats could not be launched. She sank in eighteen minutes. Of the 1,959 people aboard, 1,198 died, among them 128 Americans.

Germany argued that the ship was carrying rifle ammunition, which was true, and that it had published warnings in New York newspapers, which it had. Neither answered the outrage in the United States and in neutral opinion generally, and Berlin restricted its submarine campaign rather than risk American entry. When unrestricted submarine warfare resumed in February 1917, alongside the Zimmermann Telegram's offer of American territory to Mexico, it pushed Congress to declare war that April. The Lusitania is often called the cause; it was the start of the argument.
